transcript.text: Every time I put the oven on it runs for a few minutes and then the trip switch goes and half the house loses power. Reset it 3 times tonight. Hotpoint built-in, about 9 years old. What could cause this?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Please don't keep resetting the trip. Leave the appliance unplugged and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer before using it again. The most likely cause is a heating element whose insulation is breaking down and leaking electricity to earth once it gets hot. That fits an oven which runs briefly, then trips the circuit. It could be the fan-oven, base or grill element; the function in use does not prove which one, as the circuits can share electrical paths. Less commonly, it is heat-damaged wiring or an element terminal, with the control board further down the list. Do not use the oven again or keep resetting the trip: it needs a qualified appliance engineer or electrician to insulation-test the elements and inspect the wiring/terminals, then identify the actual leaking part. With the oven switched off and isolated, the useful observations are:
1. Note which cooking function was selected when it tripped. This helps the engineer narrow the test sequence, but does not identify the failed element by itself.
2. Without removing panels, check for any burning smell, smoke, or obvious scorching. If present, leave it isolated and mention this when booking. At around nine years old, an element fault is often repairable, but it must be confirmed by proper electrical testing before any part is chosen.

candidates: Heating element insulation leaking to earth as it heats (high)

reading.symptom: Trips the electrical circuit after a few minutes of running, cutting power to half the house

plan: They asked: "What could cause this?" - answer that first.

Safety: a supply trip hazard is active. The fixed safety warning is shown separately, do not repeat it. It must not be used again until a qualified engineer has checked it: say that plainly. You may explain the likely cause and suggest checks that are safe with it switched off and unplugged, but never say or imply that a check could make it safe to use, or that they might not need an engineer.
Checks they have done and what they found: Reset the trip switch 3 times tonight - It trips again after the oven runs for a few minutes.
Already given by the customer, never ask for it again: make Hotpoint.

The fault they reported is: "Trips the electrical circuit after a few minutes of running, cutting power to half the house". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.
They asked about something unsafe (repeated reset): do not explain how to do it; the fixed safety wording is shown separately. Offer the safe alternative.

Stage 2: the checks they reported did not fix it. Give the next check that best separates the remaining likely causes, or say what the likely faulty part is if the checks already point to one. Until a check has confirmed which part has failed, name it as the likely part and the check that would confirm it; do not tell them to buy, order or replace it.
